In [[graph theory]], the '''interval chromatic number''' <math>\chi_<(H)</math> of an [[ordered graph]] <math>H</math> is the minimum number of intervals the (linearly ordered) vertex set of <math>H</math> can be [[partition of a set|partitioned]] into so that no two vertices belonging to the same interval are adjacent in <math>H</math>.<ref name="pt05">{{citation
 | last1 = Pach | first1 = János | author1-link = János Pach

 | editor1-last = Mitchell | editor1-first = Joseph S. B.
 | editor2-last = Rote | editor2-first = Günter
 | contribution = Forbidden patterns and unit distances
 | doi = 10.1145/1064092.1064096
 | mr = 2460341
 | pages = 1–9
 | publisher = Association for Computing Machinery

 | year = 2005| s2cid = 18752227 }}</ref><ref name="nw19">{{cite journal |last1=Neidinger |first1=Dana |last2=West |first2=Douglas B. |date=September 2019 |title=Ramsey Numbers of Interval 2-Chromatic Ordered Graphs |journal=Graphs and Combinatorics |volume=35 |issue=5 |pages=1065–1076 |doi=10.1007/s00373-019-02057-8 |issn=0911-0119 |arxiv=1805.05900}}</ref>

== Definition and basic properties ==

An '''ordered graph''' is a graph <math>G</math> together with a specified [[linear ordering]] on its vertex set <math>V(G)</math>. In an ordered graph <math>H</math>, an '''interval coloring''' is a partition of <math>V(H)</math> into independent sets of consecutive vertices (called '''intervals''' or '''parts'''). The '''interval chromatic number''' <math>\chi_<(H)</math> is the minimum number of parts in any interval coloring of <math>H</math>.<ref name="nw19"/>

Since the parts of an interval coloring are independent sets:
:<math>\chi_<(H) \geq \chi(H)</math>,
where <math>\chi(H)</math> is the ordinary [[chromatic number]].<ref name="nw19"/>

An ordered graph is called '''interval k-chromatic''' (or '''k-ichromatic''') if <math>\chi_<(H) = k</math>.<ref name="nw19"/>

== Computational complexity ==

It is of particular interest that the interval chromatic number is easily computable. By a simple [[greedy algorithm]], one can efficiently find an optimal partition of the vertex set of <math>H</math> into <math>\chi_<(H)</math> independent intervals.<ref name="pt05"/> This is in sharp contrast with computing the usual chromatic number of a graph, where even finding an approximation is an [[NP hard]] task.

For a given graph <math>H</math> and its [[isomorphic]] graphs, the [[chromatic number]] remains the same, but the interval chromatic number may differ depending on the ordering of the vertex set.<ref name="nw19"/>

== Extremal theory ==

Pach and Tardos proved a fundamental theorem relating the interval chromatic number to extremal graph theory:<ref name="pt05"/>

:For any ordered graph <math>H</math>, the maximum number of edges that an <math>H</math>-free ordered graph with <math>n</math> vertices can have is:
::<math>ex_<(n, H) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{\chi_<(H) - 1}\right)\binom{n}{2} + o(n^2)</math>

This theorem naturally extends to families <math>\mathcal{H}</math> of forbidden ordered subgraphs with:<ref name="pt05"/>
:<math>\chi_<(\mathcal{H}) := \min\{\chi_<(H) \mid H \in \mathcal{H}\}</math>

== Relation to forbidden patterns ==

The interval chromatic number plays a crucial role in forbidden pattern problems for ordered graphs and zero-one matrices. For a 2-ichromatic ordered graph, the extremal problem becomes particularly interesting, as the quadratic term vanishes in the extremal function formula.<ref name="pt05"/> These can be represented by zero-one matrices where the vertices are enumerated as <math>v_1 < v_2 < \ldots < v_n < v_{n+1} < \ldots < v_{n+m}</math> such that every edge connects some <math>v_i</math> with <math>i \leq n</math> to some <math>v_j</math> with <math>j > n</math>.<ref name="pt05"/> 

The forbidden pattern problems connect to several problems in [[discrete geometry]], including the [[unit distance graph]] problem, the planar [[segment-center problem]], and the finding of [[Davenport–Schinzel sequence]]s.<ref name="pt05"/>
